To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a two-species differential atom interferometer is a promising method for a UFF test in a free-fall platform, that the statistical estimation is a key ingredient for a successful UFF test, and that a dual K/Rb interferometer in a 0-g airplane is an interesting test case.

we have shown that the differential acceleration can in principle be extracted from a two-species interferometer even in the case where the mass and the laser wavelength of the two atomic species differ by orders of magnitude.
We have developed a method for testing the weak-equivalence principle (WEP) using an atom interferometer with a large mass and wavelength difference.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) Can we measure the differential acceleration between two species of different mass and different wavelength?
the development of a two-species interferometric test of the equivalence principle, using a differential acceleration measurement between atomic species.
the development and implementation of a new method to measure the differential acceleration between two different atomic species, in a two-specie interferometric setup.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the equivalence principle is a fundamental principle of physics, and it should be tested with high accuracy, in particular in the weak-field regime.
a two-species interferometer with a large mass difference can provide a sensitive test of the weak equivalence principle, and is an ideal instrument to search for a new force.
the UFF is not violated by more than $2 \times 10^{-15}$ for the two atomic species we considered in this paper, and for a free-fall duration of about 1.5 seconds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a method to estimate the local differential acceleration using a two-species (or multi-species) atom interferometer, and that this method does not require any assumption on the platform acceleration and does not suffer from platform acceleration noise.
we have developed a new protocol for testing the weak Equivalence Principle (Universality of free fall) using an atom interferometer.
we have shown how to estimate the differential local acceleration between two atomic mixtures using atom interferometry.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a differential acceleration measurement between two atomic species is possible even in the case where the mass ratio between the atomic species is large, as long as a statistical estimation method is used.
it is possible to measure the differential acceleration between two different atoms with a large mass and wavelength difference using a single interferometer.

the statistical estimation method is a robust and simple way of extracting the differential acceleration in an atom interferometer, even in the presence of a large mass or wavelength ratio, or a large number of experimental cycles.
